text.p: Vietnam's journalists need to be educated to raise the standards of the media and assert the direction of the ruling Communist Party, Minister of Culture and Information Tran Hoan said in an interview published on Friday.
Hoan told the monthly Vietnam Economic Times that the government had decided on three measures to raise media standards to an international level.
Those measures included a drive for technical progress, investment and the creation of a stable legal environment for the media industry.

He said the government also planned "to educate and re-educate journalists to force them to have good knowledge of the Party's direction and government legislation, to possess good language skills, to be able to make good use of modern techniques, to have professionalism and a steady political belief".
Hoan said the media was an "ideological instrument" which helped improve the education of the people and encourage them to carry out policies of the party and government.
The press is regarded as highly sensitive in Vietnam and all publications come under government control.

Ahead of a party congress earlier this year, journalists were encouraged to report good news and write articles promoting socialism. In July the Interior Ministry launched probes into three prominent newspapers over alleged breaches of national security.

On Thursday, the Ha Noi Moi daily carried an official announcement that some organisations had recently contravened regulations by holding news conferences in Hanoi without seeking prior permission from the Culture and Information Department.
It said applications for a news conference needed to be submitted at least 12 hours in advance.

The choice of newspapers in Vietnam has widened dramatically since economic reforms got under way in the late 1980s, with the appearance of youth and regional journals in addition to mouthpiece publications.
The media still generally paints a glowing picture of industrial, economic or diplomatic achievements and many of their stories have a parochial slant.
However, newspaper articles critical of corruption and bureaucracy are increasingly common.
Hoan said there was now a trend towards commercialisation of the media, with publications printing "crime stories and nude pictures".

"This is 'yellow journalism', chasing profit and lowering the value of the media and it should be adjusted," he said. "The Ministry of Culture and Information has, and is, warning, criticising and adjusting this type of newspaper."
